prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "COSTCO WHOLESALE CORP /NEW" (ticker COST). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)
   "fisher": Philip Fisher (“Common Stocks and Uncommon Profits” (the 15 points, condensed))
   "graham": Benjamin Graham (“The Intelligent Investor”, criteria for the defensive investor)
   "thiel": Peter Thiel (“Zero to One”: the seven questions every business must answer)
   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))
   "greenblatt": Joel Greenblatt (“The Little Book That Beats the Market” (the Magic Formula))
   "akre": Chuck Akre (Akre's “three-legged stool”)
   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)
   "wood": Cathie Wood (ARK Invest's published research (“Big Ideas”) on disruptive innovation)
   "ackman": Bill Ackman (Pershing Square's stated investment criteria (annual letters and presentations))
   "sleep": Nick Sleep (Nomad Investment Partnership letters (2001–2014))
   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
   "nash": Tom Nash: the 12-step research process (“How to Find the Best Stocks in the Market” (Tom Nash, 2026))
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM"}

summaries.gardner: Costco is a 'Rule Maker' more than a Rule Breaker: it is the top dog in warehouse clubs with a beloved brand, but it is not a first mover in an emerging industry. Its shares rose only about 4.5% in the past year, behind the market, though commentators do routinely call it overvalued, a trait Gardner likes.
summaries.buffett: Costco fits Buffett's tenets on the business: simple, consistent (revenue up every year from $195.9B in FY2021 to $303.2B in FY2026), honest management and a durable cost-and-loyalty moat. Price is the problem: at about 46 times trailing earnings and a 2.2% free-cash-flow yield there is no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Charlie Munger sat on Costco's board from 1997 until his death in 2023 and called it one of the businesses he admired most, for its culture and scale economics shared with members. Inverting, there are few ways for it to fail, but at about 46 times earnings the price is far above what most value investors would pay.
summaries.lynch: Costco is a stalwart with fast-grower traits and a simple story (open about 30 new warehouses a year, raise membership fees occasionally, grow digital sales). Its PEG ratio of about 3.8 is well above Lynch's comfort level, and the stock is heavily followed.
summaries.fisher: Costco scores strongly on Fisher's points about employee relations, management depth, integrity and cost control, and its sales growth has lasted decades. Its very low profit margin (3.85% operating) is by design, which Fisher would accept only because it builds the moat.
summaries.graham: Costco passes Graham's tests for size, earnings stability (profitable every year) and EPS growth (diluted EPS up from $5.33 in FY2016 to $20.76 in FY2026), and has paid dividends since 2004. It fails the valuation tests badly: about 53 times three-year average earnings and P/E times P/B of about 540.
summaries.thiel: Costco has a monopoly-like position in its niche, a strong distribution system and a durable, members-first culture, scoring well on Thiel's durability and distribution questions. It has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals and operates in an old industry.
summaries.gerstner: Costco is not a technology growth company, but it has accelerating revenue (up 10.1% in FY2026), digitally-enabled sales growing about 20% and new businesses such as retail media. At about 42 times forward earnings for roughly 10% EPS growth, the valuation is demanding.
summaries.druckenmiller: Costco's earnings are growing steadily (diluted EPS up 14% to $20.76 in FY2026) and it beat Q4 FY2026 estimates, but there is no sharp earnings inflection. The stock lagged the market over the past year, which weakens the momentum case Druckenmiller looks for.
summaries.smith: Costco has many qualities Terry Smith seeks, a resilient, predictable business with ROIC of about 37% and strong cash conversion, but its gross margin of about 11-13% is far below his usual preference for high-margin companies. At about 46 times free cash flow it fails his 'don't overpay' rule.
summaries.greenblatt: Costco's return on capital is very high (ROIC about 37%), but its earnings yield is only about 2.7% at an EV/EBIT of about 36. It would not rank highly on a Magic Formula screen.
summaries.akre: Costco looks strong on all three of Akre's legs: an extraordinary business, honest and capable management with a members-first culture, and the ability to reinvest in about 30 new warehouses a year at high returns. Only the valuation is a concern.
summaries.pabrai: Costco offers a low risk of permanent loss but no Dhandho-style mispricing or temporary distress, trading at about 46 times earnings. Pabrai's deep-value setup is not present.
summaries.wood: Costco is not a leader in any of ARK's innovation platforms and its market grows slowly. It does not fit Cathie Wood's approach.
summaries.ackman: Costco matches many Pershing Square criteria: a simple, predictable, free-cash-flow generative business with dominant market position and high barriers to entry. Ackman also requires a meaningful discount to intrinsic value, which about 46 times earnings does not provide.
summaries.sleep: Costco is Nick Sleep's archetype of 'scale economies shared': Nomad owned it and described how it passes savings from its growing scale back to members, making it ever harder to compete with. Its position looks likely to strengthen over the next 10-20 years.
summaries.valentine: Costco solves a real problem, the cost of groceries and essentials, but it is a mature 43-year-old retailer rather than a fast-growing, technology-driven new market. It sits outside Don Valentine's venture approach.
summaries.nash: Costco passes most of Nash's quality checks, scoring about 90 on his scorecard thanks to its moat, culture, net cash and 10.1% revenue growth. It fails his instant-kill rule on operating margin (3.85%, far below 20%) and the valuation checks: the DCF at a 12% discount rate is far below the share price and the PEG is about 3.8.

momentum.evidence: Costco rose 4.54% over the 52 weeks to Oct 14, 2026 (about $977.66), well behind the SPY S&P 500 ETF's 17.28% one-year total return.

g4.evidence: Costco is run by company lifer Ron Vachris and was long backed by Charlie Munger, a director from 1997 until his death in 2023.

g6.evidence: At about 46 times trailing and 42 times forward earnings (StockAnalysis, Oct 2026), Costco is widely described as one of the most expensive retail stocks.

simple.evidence: It sells a limited range of goods at low markups in warehouses and earns much of its profit from annual membership fees, a model anyone can understand.

b2.evidence: Revenue rose every year from $195,929M in FY2021 to $303,154M in FY2026, and diluted EPS rose from $5.33 in FY2016 to $20.76 in FY2026.

integrity.evidence: Costco is known for candour, modest executive pay, a code of ethics that puts members and employees first, and capital returns through regular and special dividends.

b6.evidence: Costco sticks to its warehouse-club model and makes few acquisitions, growing by opening about 30 warehouses a year.

roic.evidence: Costco earns ROIC of about 37% and ROE of about 28% (StockAnalysis) with debt of only $6,162M against $21,301M of cash and short-term investments.

fcf.evidence: FY2026 free cash flow was $9,382M (operating cash flow $15,817M less capex $6,435M), about equal to net income of $9,226M.

b10.evidence: Retained earnings funded new warehouses that lifted net income from $5,844M in FY2022 to $9,226M in FY2026 and market value to about $433B.

safety.evidence: At about $977.66 the shares trade at about 46 times trailing EPS and 11.8 times book value, leaving no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: A forward P/E of about 42 for roughly 10% expected EPS growth gives a PEG of about 3.8.

mu5.evidence: With 92.3% US/Canada renewal rates, net cash and low-markup pricing that rivals struggle to undercut, there are few ways for the business to fail.

reinvest.evidence: Costco plans 33 openings in FY2027 and about 30 net new warehouses a year, reinvesting at a ROIC of about 37%.

ly2.evidence: Costco is a stalwart with a simple story: more warehouses, more members, occasional fee increases and growing digital sales.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 46 is far above its EPS growth rate (diluted EPS up 14% in FY2026), a PEG of about 3.8.

runway.evidence: It has room for many more warehouses in China, Japan, Europe, Australia and the US, plus digitally-enabled sales growing about 20% a year and retail media.

ly7.evidence: Insiders are not notable buyers and the share count is roughly flat (diluted shares 444.3M in FY2021 vs 444.4M in FY2026).

ly8.evidence: Costco is widely covered and owned, with about 74% institutional ownership.

fi2.evidence: Costco keeps adding services (gas, pharmacy, hearing aids, travel, retail media, Costco Next), but its core warehouse format changes slowly.

fi3.evidence: Costco does not report R&D spending; its innovation comes through merchandising and Kirkland Signature products.

fi4.evidence: With almost no advertising it gets 84.1 million paid members and 92.3% US/Canada renewal, and comparable sales grew 9.4% in Q4 FY2026.

longterm.evidence: Costco caps its markups and reinvested part of its Q4 FY2026 tariff refund into member value, putting long-term loyalty ahead of short-term profit.

gr1.evidence: Costco had $303,154M of FY2026 revenue and a market value of about $433B.

ni10.evidence: Costco has been profitable every year of the last ten, with net income rising from $2.35B in FY2016 to $9,226M in FY2026.

gr4.evidence: Costco has paid a quarterly dividend since 2004 and raised it for 21 consecutive years.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $5.33 in FY2016 to $20.76 in FY2026, an increase of about 290%.

gr6.evidence: At about $977.66 the price is about 53 times the FY2024-FY2026 average EPS of about $18.51.

gr7.evidence: A P/E of about 46.0 times a P/B of about 11.8 gives roughly 540, far above Graham's 22.5 limit.

th1.evidence: Costco's advantage is scale, culture and membership economics, not proprietary technology ten times better than rivals.

timing.evidence: Value-seeking consumers and inflation favour Costco, but it is not riding a new technology wave.

th3.evidence: It started in 1983 with a big share of the small US warehouse-club niche and expanded to 939 warehouses in 14 countries.

team.evidence: Costco is run by a world-class operating team that continues Jim Sinegal's model, led by CEO Ron Vachris, a 40-plus-year company veteran.

th5.evidence: Its membership model and warehouses are a powerful distribution channel that suppliers and members both depend on.

durable.evidence: Its low-cost, high-loyalty model has resisted Walmart, Amazon and Sam's Club for four decades and seems likely to hold for 10-20 more years.

th7.evidence: The warehouse-club model is well known and copied; Costco's edge is execution, not a secret opportunity.

trend.evidence: Costco is not a leading beneficiary of a platform shift such as AI or cloud computing.

dr1.evidence: Revenue growth accelerated to 10.1% in FY2026 and Q4 EPS of $6.75 beat the $6.55 consensus, but EPS growth is steady rather than accelerating sharply.

dr2.evidence: More warehouse openings and digital and retail media growth should improve results, but this is largely expected by investors.

dr4.evidence: Costco is resilient in slowdowns as shoppers trade down, but high rates and tariffs pressure consumers and its thin margins.

dr6.evidence: A future membership fee increase or a special dividend are identifiable catalysts, though their timing is unknown.

dr7.evidence: The business quality supports high conviction, but the stretched valuation limits the case for a large concentrated position now.

gm.evidence: Gross margin on net sales was about 11.1% in FY2026, deliberately low; Costco's pricing power shows in its membership fees instead.

fcfyield.evidence: The free-cash-flow yield is about 2.2% (StockAnalysis), low for roughly 10% growth.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT is about 36.4, an operating earnings yield of only about 2.7% on an enterprise value of about $422B.

pa2.evidence: There is no temporary setback; comparable sales grew 9.4% in Q4 FY2026.

pa4.evidence: Business risk is low with net cash and 92.3% renewal rates, but at about 46 times earnings a de-rating could cause a long period of losses.

wo1.evidence: Costco is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing.

wo2.evidence: Its unit costs fall with volume and it passes the savings on in lower prices, but this does not open up big new demand the way technology cost curves do.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several innovation platforms.

wo4.evidence: Its market grows slowly; revenue is expected to rise about 8% in FY2027, not many times over in five years.

ac3.evidence: Membership fees and net cash insulate it, but gasoline prices, inflation and tariffs still swing its sales and costs.

ns1.evidence: Costco caps markups at about 14-15% and keeps gross margin around 11% while growing, passing scale savings to members.

ns4.evidence: With paid members growing 3.8% a year, 30 new warehouses a year and rising digital sales, its position in 10-20 years looks clearly stronger.

va2.evidence: It eases the cost of food and essentials for 84.1 million paid member households, an important but not acutely painful problem.

tn1.evidence: Costco is a warehouse retailer, not a company built for a secular trend like AI, energy or robotics.

tn2.evidence: The market sees Costco as a high-quality membership retailer, which is what it is.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap US company and not a small cap, Chinese company, commodity producer, airline, seasonal business or startup.

tn4.evidence: It passes all three: revenue grew every year to $303,154M in FY2026, net income was $9,226M, and cash of $21,301M exceeds debt of $6,162M.

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow was positive ($9,382M in FY2026) and cash and short-term investments ($21,301M) exceeded total debt including leases ($10,181M) at fiscal year-end.

tn6.evidence: Total revenue grew 10.1% in FY2026, from $275,235M to $303,154M.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of 10.1% plus a free-cash-flow margin of 3.1% ($9,382M / $303,154M) gives about 13, far below 40.

tn8.evidence: In FY2026 revenue rose 10.1% while total costs and expenses rose about 10.0%, so operating income grew 12.5% to $11,685M.

tn9.evidence: It fails one instant kill: its operating margin of 3.85% is far below 20%; it passes on size, net cash, 1.66% short interest, growth and age.

tn10.evidence: Costco faces no major regulatory or legal threat; its notable legal matter is its own suit seeking refunds of IEEPA tariffs.

tn11.evidence: Costco provides quality groceries and goods at the lowest prices that help families and small businesses save money, charging an annual membership fee plus a small markup; members choose it for value and trust.

tn13.evidence: Total of about 90: cash vs debt 10, revenue growth (10.1%) 5, operating margin (3.85%) 0, short interest (1.66%) 10, institutional ownership (74%) 10, revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return ahead of the S&P 500 by over 20 points 10, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 10, secular trend 0, culture and mission 10, talent 10.

tn14.evidence: Revenue grew every year, operating margin rose from 3.42% (FY2021) to 3.85% (FY2026) and cash exceeded debt every year, but free cash flow dipped in FY2024 ($6,629M vs $6,745M in FY2023).

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 79x, current ratio 1.06 and liabilities 1.5x equity pass, but assets excluding goodwill ($88,092M) are only about 1.65x liabilities ($53,242M).

tn18.evidence: Ron Vachris has executed well since becoming CEO in January 2024, but he has under 10 years in the role, is not a founder and has made no notable open-market share purchases.

tn20.evidence: Costco usually meets or beats estimates; Q4 FY2026 EPS of $6.75 beat the $6.55 consensus and revenue of $95.7B beat $94.85B.

tn21.evidence: There is no clown CEO, co-CEO, acquisition spree, accounting concern or auditor change; margins are rising and inventory ($19,324M) grew more slowly than sales.

tn22.evidence: Costco has $303B of revenue, strong profits and a stable share count, the opposite of a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: At about 46 times earnings and a 2.2% FCF yield the price implies sustained growth well above the roughly 8-10% the company is delivering.

tn25.evidence: With 3-year averages of about 7.8% revenue growth and a 2.85% FCF margin, five years of FCF, 4% terminal growth and a 12% discount rate plus net cash, the value is well under half of today's roughly $433B market value.

tn26.evidence: A forward P/E of about 42 is far above peers such as Walmart (about 37) and BJ's, and the PEG of about 3.8 is far above 1.
